summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning dashboard for myself, and it's turned into the best test case I have for a specific design question: how do you let an LLM help teach a language without letting it teach anything wrong. My rule is a two-bucket split — the model can read your data and comment on it in English all day, but it never gets to generate Japanese content live. Anything in Japanese gets written offline, checked against a real tokenizer and a dictionary, and frozen before a learner ever sees it. That constraint sounds academic until you hit the actual bug it prevents: the audio pipeline synthesizes は as "wa" correctly in context, but say it in isolation and the same TTS engine reverts to "ha" — the app now patches that at the phonetic level before synthesis instead of trusting the model to know better.

Underneath that is a curriculum engine that only ever unlocks a word once every character in it has actually been taught, so nothing you're drilling contains a stranger. I run it against real data too — one grid I built (a heatmap of every character I've drilled) told me my worst columns are specific vowel sounds, at percentages I wouldn't have guessed on my own.

I've also been doing more general infrastructure work: a small FastAPI service that reads Anki's SQLite collection without corrupting it (Anki locks the file exclusive, so version-mismatched readers can silently upgrade the schema out from under the desktop app), and a few Docker deployments behind Cloudflare and Tailscale for personal tools I use daily.

Most recently I moved one of these apps off a single JSON blob to a small per-user SQLite store, mainly to get ahead of wanting to share it with family later without a rebuild — the trick was keeping the migration to one seam (how the app loads and saves state) so nothing else in the codebase had to change.
